name: Bukar Sadong
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: Simple words in Mentu Land Dayak have one, two, three or four syllables; the last syllable of a polysyllabic word behaves in the same way as as the only syllable in a monosyllabic word and phonetically is stressed. [...] In polysyllabic words the first syllable allows more vowel contrasts than any word-medial syllables and may be considered to have secondary stress (not indicated).
sweep_summary: Two works with stress in the title, both the same paper: Rensch 'Rhythm in Bidayuh' as a 2006 10-ICAL preprint (Glottolog 95762; print-only — SPLC 19 contents page recovered from the Internet Archive and saved, but no PDF of the published version exists on the SIL Philippines online list, SIL Global record 51516 is 404/503, no archived copy at the Internet Archive). The paper is about ultima vowel length and full/reduced penult vowels, with one stress sentence (p.2): 'Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation' — confirms the catalog's fixed-strict final-stress coding for Bukar-Sadung (Eastern Bidayuh). The more authoritative first-hand statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Rensch et al. 2012 (SIL e-Book 33: p.47 ultima receives the peak of word stress in citation forms, p.94 fn.79 enclitics take the stress, p.292 Land Dayak consistently accents the final syllable of the stem. Nothing read contradicts or refines the classification; it does not supersede the catalog's deciding source (Court 1972 via StressTyp2, the lect-specific phonology, still print-only). searching was done by direct downloads (SIL Philippines, the Internet Archive, Crossref, Glottolog).

new_statements.reading: Fixed final (ultima) word stress in citation forms, with enclitics taking the stress when attached; no stress contrast; the penult full/reduced vowel distinction is a historical reflex of PAN accent, not synchronic stress. Bukar-Sadung (Eastern) data are among the examples throughout (e.g. Tebakang, Bunan forms on p.47). The works with stress in the title itself (Rensch 2006 p.2, 'Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation') says the same in one sentence. Both agree with the catalog's fixed-strict final coding; the only nuance not in the catalog rule is Court's optional secondary stress on the first syllable, which Rensch does not mention.

audit.reasoning: Coding fixed-strict final stress (stress placement coded per word length as 01 101 1001 (1 = a stressed syllable)) is supported by four independent statements, three of them verified in copies we hold: McGinn 2003:44 (verbatim; 'oxytone' aside is p.37 not p.38), Rensch et al. 2012:47 (verbatim; also p.94 fn.79, p.292), Rensch 2006:2 (downloaded now), and Court 1972 via the StressTyp2 entry(verified; original print-only, not yet obtained). No source found suggests anything other than final stress; the only nuances are Court's optional secondary stress on the first syllable (catalog rule marks none) and Rensch 2012's note that enclitics take the stress in citation forms vs Court's StressTyp2 forms rəˈminəˌkuʔ with primary on the stem — a domain footnote, not a reclassify. Not 'well-sourced' only because the lect-specific primary phonology (Court 1966/1972) is held second-hand; optional housekeeping: fix McGinn locator 38 -> 37 and consider promoting Rensc
